segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this I looked, and there was a door standing open in heaven, and the first voice, the one I had heard speaking with me like a trumpet, said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I was at once in the Spirit, and there was a throne set in heaven, and on the throne someone was seated,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the one seated was like jasper and carnelian stone in appearance, and around the throne was a rainbow like emerald in appearance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and on the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From the throne come flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder; and seven torches of fire are burning before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and before the throne there is something like a sea of glass, like crystal. And in the midst of the throne and around the throne are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The first living creature is like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature has a face like a human being’s, and the fourth living creature is like an eagle in flight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and they have no rest day or night, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to the one seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the twenty-four elders fall down before the one seated on the throne and worship the one who lives forever and ever, and they cast their crowns before the throne, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive the glory and the honor and the power, for you created all things, and because of your will they existed and were created.”

notes.traditional: what must take place after this
notes.note: The Greek words for “after this” come next, and most translations attach them to the voice’s speech: “what must take place after this,” a phrase that echoes 1:19 and Daniel 2. The Greek edition translated here punctuates them as the opening of the next sentence, and the translation follows it. The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so either division is possible.

This points back to the trumpet-like voice of 1:10. There John turns toward the voice and sees the risen Jesus, so most interpreters take the speaker here to be Jesus, and the words are treated as his. Some think instead of an angel who guides John through the visions.

The Greek has no article and could also be read “in spirit,” meaning a visionary state in which John’s own spirit is caught up. Most translations, as here, take it of God’s Spirit bringing the vision about, as at 1:10. The two readings are not far apart, since the experience is prophetic inspiration either way.

notes.traditional: jasper and sardius (KJV “a jasper and a sardine stone”)
notes.note: Ancient gem names do not map exactly onto modern ones. The stone called jasper could be translucent and of various colors, and 21:11 describes it as clear as crystal. The second stone is a red gem, usually identified as carnelian. John describes the one on the throne only by radiance and color, never by form.

The text does not say who the elders are, and their identity is disputed. Common proposals are a heavenly council of angelic beings, representatives of God’s people (twelve tribes and twelve apostles), or a counterpart to the twenty-four priestly divisions of 1 Chronicles 24. Their thrones, white garments and crowns mark them as honored and as sharing in rule.

Many interpreters take this as a symbolic way of speaking of God’s one Spirit in its fullness, drawing on the seven lamps of Zechariah 4; some translations print “the sevenfold Spirit” in a footnote. Others understand seven chief angels who stand before God. The translation leaves the phrase as the Greek has it, in lowercase, without deciding.

notes.phrase: in the midst of the throne and around the throne
notes.traditional: in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne
notes.note: The Greek is as hard to picture as the English. It may mean that the creatures stand close around the throne, one at the middle of each side, or that they are in some way part of the throne itself, as the cherubim are in Ezekiel’s vision. Translations vary: “around the throne, on each side of the throne,” or “in the center, around the throne.”

notes.traditional: four beasts (KJV); four living creatures (most modern versions)
notes.note: The scene combines the four living creatures of Ezekiel 1, with their four faces and many eyes, and the six-winged seraphim of Isaiah 6, who cry “Holy, holy, holy.” The Greek word simply means a living being. It is a different word from the one used for the hostile “beast” later in the book.

The verbs in verses 9–10 are future in Greek: literally “whenever the living creatures will give … the elders will fall.” Most translators take this as describing what happens repeatedly, perhaps reflecting a Hebrew way of expressing customary action, and so use the English present. Some read it as a real future, pointing ahead to the worship described in the chapters that follow.

notes.traditional: O Lord (KJV, following a different manuscript reading); our Lord and God
notes.note: The Roman writer Suetonius reports that the emperor Domitian liked to be addressed as “our lord and god.” Many scholars think the first hearers in Asia Minor would have heard this acclamation as a claim that such titles belong to God alone. Whether John intends a direct allusion is uncertain, since the pairing also has roots in the Greek Old Testament.

candidates.reason: Must stay distinct from θηρίον (“beast”) throughout Revelation, and the KJV’s “beasts” for both shows how easily the two are confused; it also occurs in Hebrews, 2 Peter and Jude for animals.
A recurring divine title (nine times in Revelation and 2 Cor 6:18) where translators choose between “Almighty,” “All-Powerful” and “Ruler of all,” and the reader should see one title.

Used across the Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation for Jewish leaders, church officers, older men and the heavenly twenty-four; a single decision on “elder” versus “older man” or “presbyter” by sense is needed.
Extremely frequent across narrative and vision; versions vary between “behold,” “look,” “see,” restructuring and omission, and the handling should be uniform.

candidates.rendering: Spirit (in the phrase “in the Spirit”); spirits (of the seven spirits of God)
candidates.reason: Capitalization and the choice between “in the Spirit” and “in spirit” for the anarthrous ἐν πνεύματι, and for the seven spirits, need to be settled once for Revelation and the letters.
